title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
keyIdea: The stop limit breaks plain Dijkstra (a cheap route may have too many stops). BFS by number of flights with (stops, city, cost) and a best-price array, skipping entries past k stops; or Bellman-Ford for k + 1 rounds, each reading only the previous round's prices.

approaches.name: Bellman-Ford, k + 1 rounds
approaches.idea: dist[src] = 0; repeat k + 1 times: next = dist; relax every flight from dist into next; dist = next.
approaches.why: k + 1 passes over all flights; the copy keeps it to one more flight per round.

approaches.name: BFS by number of stops
approaches.idea: Queue (stops, city, cost); skip stops > k; a flight that lowers dist[city] updates it and queues (stops + 1, city, newCost).
approaches.why: Each level of BFS is one more flight; there are at most k + 1 levels.

quiz.q: Why can plain Dijkstra give a wrong answer here?
options: It keeps only the cheapest way to each city, which may already use too many stops

quiz.q: k stops means how many flights at most?
In Bellman-Ford, why copy dist into next each round?
options: So a round can't chain two flights using a price updated in the same round

quiz.q: In the BFS version, what happens to a queue entry with stops > k?
options: It is skipped: flying further would exceed the stop limit
